idiom_name: java.nio Selector reactor plus a fixed ExecutorService draining a BlockingQueue
implementation_notes: The asynchronous layer is a Selector reactor thread that registers interest and never performs blocking I/O; decoded requests go into a BlockingQueue whose bound is the back-pressure control point, and the synchronous layer is a fixed ExecutorService whose tasks take() from the queue and run the blocking business or JDBC code. Each layer keeps its own synchronisation policy, which is exactly the pattern's separation of concerns. This is the structure Java frameworks such as Netty and Vert.x build internally; on Java 21 the virtual-thread variant makes most of it unnecessary.
pitfalls: Blocking inside the selector thread - a JDBC call, a contended lock, even a slow decode - removes the asynchronous layer's advantage and serialises every connection.
An unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue turns overload into heap pressure; bound it and choose the rejection policy deliberately.
Mixing CompletableFuture chains with take() loops in one pool causes thread-pool starvation; the JDK virtual-thread guide warns explicitly against mixing blocking code with asynchronous frameworks.

variants.name: Virtual threads with plain blocking service code
variants.idiom_name: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() with blocking I/O in the thread-per-request style
variants.implementation_notes: On Java 21 the runtime supplies the asynchronous layer: when code running in a virtual thread blocks on I/O the virtual thread unmounts from its carrier, so the operating-system thread is freed and the thread-per-request style scales without a Selector, an ExecutorService pool or an explicit queue. Concurrency against a shared resource is then capped with a Semaphore rather than a pool, and explicit BlockingQueues remain only where work must cross stages or survive a restart. Keep the blocking synchronous style pure: the JDK guide advises not to mix it with asynchronous frameworks.
pitfalls: Blocking inside a synchronized block or a native call pins the virtual thread to its carrier and can starve the scheduler.
Virtual threads must not be pooled or treated as reusable resources; ThreadLocal caches meant for pooled threads misbehave.
Long CPU-bound work still needs a bounded pool: virtual threads provide throughput, not speed.
